questions.q: A Pod won't start. What is the recommended first command to run, and why?
options: kubectl logs, because the application's own error message is always the cause
kubectl describe, because its Events section shows what the cluster actually tried (image pulls, scheduling, restarts)
kubectl delete, to immediately remove the broken Pod
kubectl exec, to manually start the container's process
questions.explain: describe's Events section shows cluster-level problems like failed image pulls or scheduling failures — often the real cause before the container ever runs, which logs can't show.

questions.q: Why is `kubectl apply -f file.yaml` generally preferred over imperative commands like `kubectl create` or `kubectl run`?
options: apply is faster to type
apply only works on Deployments, not other objects
apply is declarative and safe to run repeatedly — it only changes what differs between the file and the cluster's current state
create and run have been removed from kubectl entirely
questions.explain: apply reconciles the cluster toward what the file describes, so running it again with no changes does nothing — consistent with Kubernetes's declarative model.

questions.q: What is the difference between `kubectl logs` and `kubectl exec`?
options: They are identical commands with different names
logs shows what a container has already printed to stdout/stderr; exec runs a new command inside the container right now
logs only works on Deployments; exec only works on Pods
exec shows past output; logs starts an interactive shell
questions.explain: logs is read-only output review. exec actively runs a command (such as an interactive shell) inside the container at this moment — useful for investigation, not a fix for a bad image or manifest.

questions.q: You run `kubectl get pods` and see no results, even though you know the Pod exists. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Kubernetes silently deletes Pods after a few minutes
The Pod is in a different namespace than the one your command defaulted to
kubectl get pods only works once per hour
The cluster has crashed
questions.explain: Forgetting the `-n <namespace>` flag is one of the most common sources of "nothing exists" confusion — the object exists, just in a namespace other than the default one being checked.

questions.q: What does `kubectl logs checkout-pod -c payment-sidecar` do?
options: Deletes the payment-sidecar container
Shows logs for one specific container (payment-sidecar) inside a multi-container Pod
Creates a new sidecar container
Lists all containers in the cluster named payment-sidecar
questions.explain: The -c flag targets one container by name inside a Pod that runs more than one container, since `logs` needs to know which container's output to show.
